prompt.en: A path sketch is revised with both a higher refracting region and a higher antenna launch angle. Which conclusion about the first return point follows without more geometry?

text.en: It must move farther away because layer height is the only relevant change.

feedback.en: A higher region lengthens the path at fixed angle, but the launch angle also changed.

text.en: It must move closer because launch angle is the only relevant change.

feedback.en: A higher launch angle shortens skip at fixed region height, but the height also changed.
Opposing trends do not establish equal effects. Their sizes matter.

text.en: The two changes act in opposite directions, so their net effect needs more information.

feedback.en: More height tends to lengthen skip while a higher launch angle tends to shorten it. Neither fixed-condition rule settles the combined change.

explanation.en: Keep the fixed conditions attached to each trend. A combined change needs more geometry than either trend alone.

prompt.en: A shoreline ground-wave route is moved much higher in frequency while the checkpoints stay fixed. Which revised expectation fits?

text.en: Useful surface-wave coverage may shrink, so the old checkpoint route may need a different band or path.

feedback.en: Ground wave is most useful at lower frequencies. The same checkpoint route may need a lower band or a different path.

text.en: That higher frequency follows terrain more closely and automatically extends ground-wave coverage.

feedback.en: That reverses the frequency trend. Higher-frequency ground wave is usually less useful over the same surface route.

text.en: That a higher band automatically replaces the surface path with an F2 return at the same checkpoints.

feedback.en: A useful sky-wave path depends on frequency, ionization, and geometry; it does not automatically serve the old ground-wave area.

text.en: That only antenna size changes, leaving useful ground-wave range fixed.

feedback.en: Frequency affects propagation as well as antenna dimensions.

explanation.en: Do not carry a coverage map from a lower-frequency surface path onto a much higher band without new evidence.

prompt.en: A multi-hop sketch adds enough hop distance to span a route. Why should the agency still avoid treating it as assured backup coverage?

text.en: Distance arithmetic alone guarantees coverage if every hop scale was added correctly.

feedback.en: That checks only map distance, not current ionization, launch angles, or losses.

text.en: Each extra surface return can add loss, and the required ionospheric path still has to exist.

feedback.en: A geometrically long enough plan can still fail when conditions or link strength are unsuitable.

text.en: All hops retain the original signal strength because surface reflection restores energy.

feedback.en: Reflection redirects some energy; it does not regenerate the signal or replace losses.

text.en: Increasing power guarantees that every planned sky-wave return occurs at the drawn point.

feedback.en: Power can affect link strength but does not set the return geometry.

explanation.en: Hop scales support an initial plan. Listening and path evidence are still needed before relying on it.
